o: A substring is semi-repetitive if it contains at most one pair of adjacent equal digits. Scanning `s`, each boundary `i` (between positions `i-1` and `i`) is a "bad pair" if `s[i]==s[i-1]`. A window is valid while it contains at most one such boundary. Since validity is monotone (shrinking a window never adds bad pairs), a classic two-pointer / sliding window over boundaries solves it. Example "52233": boundaries 22 and 33 are bad; the longest window with ≤1 bad boundary is "5223" (length 4). "1111111": every adjacent pair is bad, so the best window covers exactly one boundary → length 2. With `n ≤ 50` even O(n²) brute force passes, but the sliding window is O(n) and generalizes.
k: Track the count of adjacent-equal boundaries inside the window; shrink from the left whenever it exceeds 1.
When shrinking past a boundary formed by s[l] and s[l+1], decrement the counter.

a.n: Approach 1: Sliding Window over Bad Boundaries
a.i: Maintain window [l, r] and the number of indices i in (l, r] with s[i]==s[i-1]. Extend r; while the count exceeds 1, advance l, decrementing when the pair (l, l+1) was bad. Record the maximum window length.
s: For each r from 1 to n-1: if s[r]==s[r-1], bad += 1.
While bad > 1: if s[l]==s[l+1], bad -= 1; l += 1.
Update ans = max(ans, r-l+1); return ans.
a.t: O(n) — each pointer moves forward at most n times

a.n: Approach 2: Brute Force Over All Substrings
a.i: With n ≤ 50, checking every start/end pair and counting adjacent duplicates inside is fast enough and easiest to reason about.
s: For each start i, extend end j, maintaining a running count of adjacent equal pairs.
If the count exceeds 1, stop extending from i.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — all start/end pairs

w: Use the sliding window in an interview; mention brute force only as a sanity baseline. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty/single-char case (answer ≥ 1), and decrementing the bad counter incorrectly when the left pointer sits exactly on a bad boundary. Follow-ups: allow at most k bad pairs (generalize the threshold), or stream the input (window approach adapts directly).
